# add-package command

Add a package to an SPDX document, or enhance the same package (workflow
only).
Tags: reference

`add-package` adds a package to an SPDX document. It runs only as a
workflow step:

```yaml
- command: add-package
  inputs:
    spdx: <spdx.json>             # SPDX file name
    package:                      # New package information
      id: <id>                    # New package ID
      name: <name>                # New package name
      download: <download-url>    # New package download URL
      version: <version>          # Optional package version
      filename: <filename>        # Optional package filename
      supplier: <supplier>        # Optional package supplier
      originator: <originator>    # Optional package originator
      homepage: <homepage>        # Optional package homepage
      copyright: <copyright>      # Optional package copyright
      summary: <summary>          # Optional package summary
      description: <description>  # Optional package description
      license: <license>          # Optional package license
      purl: <package-url>         # Optional package purl
      cpe23: <cpe-identifier>     # Optional package cpe23
    relationships:                # Optional relationships
      - type: <relationship>      # Relationship type
        element: <element>        # Related element
        comment: <comment>        # Optional comment
```

both the concluded and the declared license; it and `copyright` default

# add-relationship command

Add relationships between elements of an SPDX document.
Tags: reference

`add-relationship` adds relationships from one element of an SPDX
document to others. On the command line it adds one:

```text
spdx-tool add-relationship <spdx.json> <id> <type> <element> [comment]
```

As a workflow step it adds a list:

```yaml
- command: add-relationship
  inputs:
    spdx: <spdx.json>             # SPDX file name
    id: <id>                      # Element ID
    replace: true                 # Replace existing relationships (default: true)
    relationships:
      - type: <relationship>      # Relationship type
        element: <element>        # Related element
        comment: <comment>        # Optional comment
```

The `type` describes the relationship of `id` to `element`; both are
element IDs, such as `SPDXRef-Library`. The types are those of the SPDX
specification, such as `DESCRIBES`, `CONTAINS`, `DEPENDS_ON`,
`DEPENDENCY_OF`, `STATIC_LINK`, or `BUILD_TOOL_OF`.
The command that `spdx-tool help commands add-relationship --example add` prints adds one.

**Replace.** In a workflow, `replace` defaults to `true`: an existing
relationship between the same two elements is removed first, whatever
its type, so the step can change the type. The command line never
replaces; it adds the relationship next to any existing one.

## Examples

- add [command]: Record that the library is statically linked into the
  application, with a comment.

Print them in full with: spdx-tool help commands add-relationship --examples,
  or one alone with: spdx-tool help commands add-relationship --example
  <name>.

## See also

- spdx-tool help spdx-documents
  What an SPDX document holds, and how the tool reads and changes it.

# copy-package command

Copy a package from one SPDX document to another.
Tags: reference

`copy-package` copies a package from one SPDX document to another, for
example to merge the SBOM of a library into the SBOM of an application.
On the command line:

```text
spdx-tool copy-package <from.spdx.json> <to.spdx.json> <package> [recursive] [files]
```

As a workflow step:

```yaml
- command: copy-package
  inputs:
    from: <from.spdx.json>        # Source SPDX file name
    to: <to.spdx.json>            # Destination SPDX file name
    package: <package>            # Package ID
    recursive: true               # Optional recursive flag
    files: true                   # Optional copy-files flag
    relationships:                # Optional relationships
      - type: <relationship>      # Relationship type
        element: <element>        # Related element
        comment: <comment>        # Optional comment
```

`<package>` is the ID of the package in the source document. Only the
destination document is changed. The command that `spdx-tool help commands copy-package --example copy` prints
copies one package.

**Options.** `recursive` also copies the child packages, those that a
relationship such as `CONTAINS` or `DEPENDS_ON` places below the
package, and their children, with those relationships. `files` also
copies the files of the package. Any other option word is an error.

**Same package.** When the destination already has a package with the
same name and version, that package is enhanced instead of duplicated.

**Relationships.** In a workflow, `relationships` relate the copied
package to elements of the destination, as in `add-package`. On the
command line, add them afterward with `add-relationship`.

## Examples

- copy [command]: Copy the package SPDXRef-Json of lib.spdx.json into
  sbom.spdx.json.

Print them in full with: spdx-tool help commands copy-package --examples, or
  one alone with: spdx-tool help commands copy-package --example <name>.

## See also

- spdx-tool help commands add-relationship
[truncated]

# find-package command

Find the ID of the one package of an SPDX document that matches search
criteria.
Tags: reference

`find-package` finds the package that matches every given criterion and
prints its ID. On the command line give at least one criterion:

```text
spdx-tool find-package <spdx.json> <criteria>...
```

The criteria are `key=value` words with these keys:

- `id=<id>`: the package ID
- `name=<name>`: the package name
- `version=<version>`: the package version
- `filename=<filename>`: the package file name
- `download=<url>`: the package download location

As a workflow step, the criteria are inputs and the ID is saved in the
variable named by `output`:

```yaml
- command: find-package
  inputs:
    output: <variable>            # Output variable for package ID
    spdx: <spdx.json>             # SPDX file name
    id: <id>                      # Optional package ID
    name: <name>                  # Optional package name
    version: <version>            # Optional package version
    filename: <filename>          # Optional package filename
    download: <url>               # Optional package download URL
```

**Matching.** A value may use the wildcards `*` (any text) and `?` (one
character), and is compared without regard to case, as the command that
`spdx-tool help commands find-package --example wildcard` prints shows. Exactly one package must match: no match, or
more than one, is an error that lists the criteria and exits 1. Quote a
criterion that contains a space, as in `spdx-tool help commands find-package --example by-name`.

## Examples

- by-name [command]: Print the ID of the package named Example Library.
- wildcard [command]: Match with a wildcard; the pattern must still match
  exactly one package.

Print them in full with: spdx-tool help commands find-package --examples, or
  one alone with: spdx-tool help commands find-package --example <name>.

## See also

- spdx-tool help commands get-version
  Print the version of the one package of an SPDX document that matches search
  criter
[truncated]

# hash command

Write the SHA-256 hash of a file to a sidecar file, or verify a file against
it.
Tags: reference

`hash` generates or verifies the hash of any file. On the command line
it takes exactly three arguments:

```text
spdx-tool hash generate sha256 <file>
spdx-tool hash verify sha256 <file>
```

As a workflow step:

```yaml
- command: hash
  inputs:
    operation: generate           # generate or verify
    algorithm: sha256
    file: <file>
```

`sha256` is the only algorithm. `generate` writes the hash as lowercase
hexadecimal text to `<file>.sha256`, as the command that `spdx-tool help commands hash --example generate`
prints shows. `verify` reads that file, in either case, hashes the file
again, and prints `Sha256 Digest OK for '<file>'`, as in the command
that `spdx-tool help commands hash --example verify` prints.

**Errors.** A missing file or sidecar file, or a hash that does not
match (`Sha256 hash mismatch for '<file>'`), exits 1. Another algorithm
or operation is a usage error.

## Examples

- generate [command]: Write the SHA-256 hash of sbom.spdx.json to
  sbom.spdx.json.sha256.
- verify [command]: Check sbom.spdx.json against the hash that generate wrote.

Print them in full with: spdx-tool help commands hash --examples, or one alone
  with: spdx-tool help commands hash --example <name>.

## See also

- spdx-tool help commands
  The commands of the tool, which run from the command line or as workflow
  steps.

# query command

Run a program and print a value that a regular expression captures from its
output.
Tags: reference

`query` runs a program, searches its output for a regular expression,
and prints the text of the expression's `value` group. A workflow uses
it to put a tool version into a variable. On the command line:

```text
spdx-tool query <pattern> <program> [args]...
```

The command that `spdx-tool help commands query --example dotnet-version` prints shows one. As a workflow
step the value is saved in the variable named by `output`:

```yaml
- command: query
  inputs:
    output: <variable>
    pattern: <regex with 'value' capture>
    program: <program>
    arguments:
      - <argument>
      - <argument>
```

**Matching.** Standard output and standard error are searched line by
line, and the first line where the `value` group captures text wins.
The exit code of the program is ignored.

**Errors.** A pattern without a `(?<value>...)` group, or one that is not
a valid regular expression, is a usage error. A program that cannot be
started, or output without a match, exits 1.

## Examples

- dotnet-version [command]: Print the version of the .NET SDK that `dotnet
  --version` reports.

Print them in full with: spdx-tool help commands query --examples, or one
  alone with: spdx-tool help commands query --example <name>.

## See also

- spdx-tool help workflow-files
  Write a YAML workflow that runs commands in order with parameters and
  variables.

# rename-id command

Rename an element ID in an SPDX document, and every reference to it.
Tags: reference

`rename-id` gives an element of an SPDX document a new ID and updates
every reference to it: in relationships, in the file lists of packages,
in snippets, and in the list of elements that the document describes.
On the command line it takes exactly three arguments:

```text
spdx-tool rename-id <spdx.json> <old-id> <new-id>
```

As a workflow step:

```yaml
- command: rename-id
  inputs:
    spdx: <spdx.json>             # SPDX file name
    old: <old-id>                 # Old element ID
    new: <new-id>                 # New element ID
```

The command that `spdx-tool help commands rename-id --example rename` prints renames one package.

**Rules.** Neither ID may be empty or `SPDXRef-DOCUMENT`, which names
the document itself; that is a usage error. The new ID must not already
belong to a package, file, or snippet: `Element ID <new-id> is already
used` exits 1.

## Examples

- rename [command]: Rename the package ID SPDXRef-Library to SPDXRef-Lib.

Print them in full with: spdx-tool help commands rename-id --examples, or one
  alone with: spdx-tool help commands rename-id --example <name>.

- spdx-tool help spdx-documents

# run-workflow command

Run the steps of a workflow file or URL, with parameters, and return its
variables.
Tags: reference

`run-workflow` runs the steps of a workflow file; `spdx-tool help workflow-files`
describes the format and has a sample with runnable commands. On the
command line give a file or an `http://` or `https://` URL:

```text
spdx-tool run-workflow <workflow.yaml> [name=value]... [--verbose]
```

Each `name=value` sets a parameter that the workflow declares; an
undeclared one exits 1 with `parameter <name> not defined`. `--verbose`
prints the workflow's variables after the last step, under `Outputs:`.

As a workflow step it runs another workflow:

```yaml
- command: run-workflow
  inputs:
    file: <workflow.yaml>         # Optional workflow file
    url: <url>                    # Optional workflow url
    nuget: <package:version>      # Optional NuGet package
    integrity: <sha256>           # Optional workflow integrity check
    parameters:
      name: <value>               # Optional workflow parameter
    outputs:
      name: <variable>            # Optional output to save to variable
```

**Source.** Give exactly one of `file` and `url`. With `nuget`, as in
`DemaConsulting.Example:1.0.0`, the package is fetched into the NuGet
cache and `file` is the path of the workflow inside it.
`integrity` is the SHA-256 of the workflow file as hexadecimal text; a
different file exits 1 with `Integrity check of <source> failed`.

**Parameters and outputs.** `parameters` sets declared parameters of the
inner workflow and expands variables of the outer one. Each entry of
`outputs` copies an inner variable (the key) into an outer variable
(the value).

## See also

- spdx-tool help workflow-files
  Write a YAML workflow that runs commands in order with parameters and
  variables.

# set-variable command

Set a workflow variable from text that may use other variables (workflow
only).
Tags: reference

`set-variable` sets a variable of the running workflow. It runs only as
a workflow step:

```yaml
- command: set-variable
  inputs:
    value: <value>                # New value
    output: <variable>            # Variable to set
```

`value` is expanded first, so it can combine other variables, as in
`${{ app-id }} ${{ app-version }}`; `output` is the variable name, taken
as written. Later steps read the variable as `${{ <variable> }}`, and a
parent workflow can read it through `outputs`; see `spdx-tool help workflow-files`.

On the command line the command exits 1 with
`'set-variable' command is only valid in a workflow`.

## See also

- spdx-tool help workflow-files
  Write a YAML workflow that runs commands in order with parameters and
  variables.

result.stdout:
# to-markdown command

Write a Markdown summary of an SPDX document, with its packages and tools.
Tags: reference

`to-markdown` writes a Markdown summary of an SPDX document, for example
for a release report. On the command line:

```text
spdx-tool to-markdown <spdx.json> <out.md> [title] [depth]
```

As a workflow step:

```yaml
- command: to-markdown
  inputs:
    spdx: <spdx.json>             # SPDX file name
    markdown: <out.md>            # Output markdown file
    title: <title>                # Optional title
    depth: <depth>                # Optional heading depth
```

The title defaults to `SPDX Document` and the heading level of the title
to 2; the sections are one level deeper. The depth must be 1 or more.
The command that `spdx-tool help commands to-markdown --example summary` prints writes `### Example SBOM`.

**Content.** A table of the file name, document name, the numbers of
files, packages, and relationships, the creation time, and the creators,
then a table of name, version, and license for each of these sections:

- `Root Packages`: the packages that the document describes
- `Packages`: the other packages, apart from tools
- `Tools`: packages related as build, development, or test tools

A section without packages is left out.

## Examples

- summary [command]: Write the summary of sbom.spdx.json to sbom.md with a
  title and level-3 headings.

Print them in full with: spdx-tool help commands to-markdown --examples, or
  one alone with: spdx-tool help commands to-markdown --example <name>.

## See also

- spdx-tool help commands diagram
  Write a Mermaid entity-relationship diagram of the packages of an SPDX
  document.
- spdx-tool help spdx-documents
  What an SPDX document holds, and how the tool reads and changes it.

# update-package command

Change fields of an existing package of an SPDX document (workflow only).
Tags: reference

`update-package` changes fields of a package that the SPDX document
already has, found by its ID. It runs only as a workflow step:

```yaml
- command: update-package
  inputs:
    spdx: <spdx.json>             # SPDX file name
    package:                      # Package information
      id: <id>                    # Package ID
      name: <name>                # Optional new package name
      download: <download-url>    # Optional new package download URL
      version: <version>          # Optional new package version
      filename: <filename>        # Optional new package filename
      supplier: <supplier>        # Optional new package supplier
      originator: <originator>    # Optional new package originator
      homepage: <homepage>        # Optional new package homepage
      copyright: <copyright>      # Optional new package copyright
      summary: <summary>          # Optional new package summary
      description: <description>  # Optional new package description
      license: <license>          # Optional new package license
```

Only the given fields change. `license` sets both the concluded and the
declared license. A value such as `Organization: Example Corp` contains
`: `, so quote it in YAML.

**Errors.** A package ID that the document does not have exits 1 with
`Package '<id>' not found in <spdx.json>`, and any other key exits 1
with `Invalid package update key '<key>'`; neither changes the file.

The sample workflow in `spdx-tool help workflow-files` sets a version and a supplier
this way. On the command line the command exits 1 with
`'update-package' command is only valid in a workflow`.

  Add a package to an SPDX document, or enhance the same package (workflow
  only).
- spdx-tool help workflow-files
  Write a YAML workflow that runs commands in order with parameters and
  variables.

# validate command

Check an SPDX document against the SPDX rules, and optionally the NTIA minimum
elements.
Tags: reference

`validate` checks an SPDX document and prints one line for each issue it
finds. On the command line:

```text
spdx-tool validate <spdx.json> [ntia]
```

As a workflow step:

```yaml
- command: validate
  inputs:
    spdx: <spdx.json>             # SPDX file name
    ntia: true                    # Optional NTIA checking
```

Without issues the command prints nothing more and exits 0, as the
command that `spdx-tool help commands validate --example validate` prints shows. With issues it ends with
`Error: Found <n> Issues in <spdx.json>` and exits 1, which fails a
workflow at that step.

**NTIA.** `ntia` also checks the minimum elements of an SBOM that the
NTIA defines, such as a supplier for every package. On the command line
the word must be lowercase `ntia`; any other word is ignored. In a
workflow, `ntia: true` in any case turns it on. The command that
`spdx-tool help commands validate --example ntia` prints finds the missing suppliers of the example SBOM.

## Examples

- validate [command]: Check the document against the SPDX rules. Exits 0 when
  it has no issues.
- ntia [command]: Also check the NTIA minimum elements; the example packages
  have no supplier. Exits 1.

Print them in full with: spdx-tool help commands validate --examples, or one
  alone with: spdx-tool help commands validate --example <name>.

## See also

- spdx-tool help spdx-documents
  What an SPDX document holds, and how the tool reads and changes it.
- spdx-tool help troubleshooting
  What the exit codes mean, and how to fix the common error messages.
